documents: Equipment and Station Operating Reference. When to consult: Variable cycle times, station-to-station delays, differing spindle speeds, occasional idle periods. Possible causes: A normal process can differ by station; a bottleneck is not automatically a mechanical fault. Recommended checks: Identify the station and its running, idle or down state. Each station has its own nominal spindle speed and typical processing time per job, recorded on that station's setup sheet, which is kept with the machine and not reproduced in this manual. Speeds differ from station to station, so a speed means nothing without that station's own normal: judge a station against its own earlier behaviour, not against another station. Review several jobs before judging cycle time; single jobs naturally vary. Follow a job ID through the line to distinguish machine processing from downstream blocking. How to interpret: The line contains 3 to 8 stations. The second station has the longest nominal processing time on the default line, so some waiting before it is normal. Confirm the installed line size and current state before acting.

Measurements, Trends, Alarms and Evidence Quality. When to consult: A sensor exceeds an alarm value; averages disagree across windows; a trend looks erratic or has gaps. Possible causes: Operating changes, transient disturbances, instrument issues or developing equipment problems. Recommended checks: Compare vibration (mm/s), machine temperature (°F), motor load (%), and factory air temperature (°F) over the same relevant time window. Record ticks, sample counts, minimum and maximum, and a trend, not only the last reading. Separate running from idle periods. Link alarms to the underlying sensor readings and independent evidence. How to interpret: The default line vibration alarm is triggered by a reading above 4.5 mm/s. It is a monitoring setpoint, not a confirmed failure threshold. Missing samples are unknown, never zero. A sensor reading and a maintenance note are evidence; neither is a diagnosis. Observable channels and records: vibration (mm/s per station; speed, load and instruments affect readings); temperature (°F per station; thermal lag, compare factory air); load (% per station; active machining against idle matters); air temperature (°F, factory-wide; door and daily variation); power (kW per station; cutting load and speed, plus friction or a straining drive); following error (µm per station, the feed axis's lag behind its commanded path; §2.14); hydraulic pressure (bar, only on stations fitted with hydraulics; §2.15); events and job history (alarms, job movement, stops; events record observations, not causes); inspections (job, batch, pass or fail; outcomes are statistical); settings and maintenance (the current speed only, and service notes; service history is not present health).

Abnormal Vibration: Spike, Step Change or Gradual Rise. When to consult: One high vibration alarm; recurring peaks; a sustained increase in mm/s during production. Possible causes: Heavier workpiece load, speed change, spindle-bearing deterioration, imbalance, loose mounting, alignment, cutting chatter, or sensor disturbance. Recommended checks: Check whether the machine was running. Compare several consecutive readings and trend windows at similar loads and spindle speeds; look for changes in temperature or load. Check nearby stations for shared effects. Review operating events, setting changes, and prior maintenance. Request a physical inspection when telemetry does not separate mechanical vibration from sensor movement. How to interpret: A single spike without corroboration does not justify a repair. A persistent change across independent signals merits deeper investigation. Do not diagnose a bearing by vibration alone. See §2.2, §2.4 and §2.11.

Spindle Bearing: Wear Assessment and Replacement. When to consult: Increasing vibration, elevated operating temperature, longer machining time, worsening finish, unusual noise or a machine stop. Possible causes: Bearing wear or damage, excessive load or speed, improper lubrication, incorrect installation, and similar-looking faults elsewhere. Recommended checks: Compare vibration and temperature during like-for-like operating periods; check current speed, motor load and cycle-time trends. Review the maintenance record, but do not assume a recently serviced bearing is healthy. A technician may verify play, noise, lubrication state and physical bearing condition under a safe lockout procedure. How to interpret: If the evidence supports bearing damage and intervention is warranted, request approved replacement. A running machine may require less downtime than an already failed one: planned replacement takes roughly 45 ticks and repair after a breakdown roughly 135 ticks. Verify after the work that behaviour improves under comparable production conditions. A bearing inspection after removal is stronger evidence than an alarm.

Lubrication Condition and Contamination. When to consult: Spindle heating, rubbing sounds, increasing resistance, premature bearing wear, intermittent chatter. Possible causes: Low supply, incorrect lubricant, degraded grease or oil, contaminated lubrication, blocked distribution or excessive fill. Recommended checks: Consult service history and the lubrication schedule. When a technician can access the machine, check lubricant identity, condition, levels, delivery points and contamination under the plant safety procedure. Compare symptoms against load, speed and thermal behaviour before assigning cause. Record what was actually observed rather than assuming the lubrication circuit is defective. How to interpret: The provided sensor list does not establish oil pressure, grease flow or chemistry. Lack of an oil-pressure alarm is not evidence that lubrication is sound. Do not authorize adding lubricant, opening guards or running a dry machine solely from a model inference.

Alignment, Mounting Looseness and Rotor Imbalance. When to consult: Repeated vibration, finish variation, speed-dependent noise or a change after tooling or spindle service. Possible causes: Shaft or coupling misalignment, imbalanced workholding, loose foundation or mounting hardware, excessive runout, damaged tooling. Recommended checks: Compare vibration at comparable motor loads and speed settings. Review whether behaviour began after maintenance, tool changes or workholding adjustments. If a technician is available, check alignment, runout, fastener condition and rotating balance with suitable instruments while following lockout procedures. How to interpret: A scalar vibration trend cannot identify frequency bands, harmonics, direction or runout. Treat this as a candidate cause until an appropriate physical measurement distinguishes it from bearing wear, cutting chatter or sensor error.

Machine Temperature: Thermal Lag and Rising Heat. When to consult: Machine temperature increases over many readings; temperature is high shortly after a workload shift; temperature drops after shutdown. Possible causes: Normal motor and spindle heating, ambient air changes, increased load or speed, bearing friction, inadequate coolant flow or sensor error. Recommended checks: Compare machine temperature with factory air temperature, motor load, machine status and spindle speed over a sufficiently long interval. A stopped machine cools toward ambient; a running machine typically runs warmer. Check whether the temperature change follows a load change or begins during idle. Assess trend direction rather than reacting to one measurement. How to interpret: Thermal response is delayed. A persistent temperature rise with independent vibration or quality changes has different implications from a matched rise in factory air. Do not interpret every warm machine as a failed bearing.

Coolant Supply, Circulation and Machining Heat. When to consult: Poor surface finish, workpiece heat damage, chip accumulation, abnormal machining temperature or recurring heat-related defects. Possible causes: Insufficient or misdirected coolant, depleted tank, pump or filter trouble, incorrect mixture, obstructed nozzle, leakage or normal load changes. Recommended checks: Request a maintenance check of tank level, fluid condition, flow at the cutting zone, nozzle aim, filtration and leakage. Correlate with machine temperature, tool condition, motor load and inspection outcomes. Compare products made with the same material and similar cutting conditions. How to interpret: A general machine temperature sensor cannot establish coolant flow. No dedicated coolant-flow or coolant-pressure observation should be assumed. Record suspected causes as unconfirmed until physical checks support them.

Spindle Speed Configuration and Machining Effects. When to consult: Cycle times or quality change on one station; more or less vibration or heat after a setup; unexpectedly fast or slow work at one station. Possible causes: Incorrect program or setup speed, operator setting mistake, incorrect tooling recommendation, speed variation under load or mechanical drag. Recommended checks: The settings record shows a station's current speed only; its nominal speed is on the station's setup sheet, not in the shared records. So find a wrong setting from its effects. First, look for a change point: on one station, job times, temperature and inspection rejects shift at about the same moment and then stay at their new level, unlike wear, which keeps getting worse. Second, read the direction: a speed set too high shortens jobs and adds a little vibration and heat; a speed set too low lengthens jobs and takes a little vibration and heat away; either way, more jobs fail inspection. A worn bearing, by contrast, lengthens jobs while vibration rises. Third, compare with the other stations: a material problem spreads across stations that handle the same batch, a setting stays on one station. Verify that a slow cycle is not simply a downstream blockage (§2.8). How to interpret: A change point with these effects on one station is a configuration clue, not proof that it caused every anomaly. The corrective action is an approved setting reset, which stops the station for about 10 ticks and returns it to its nominal speed. Because it is short and reversible, it is also a test: if job times, temperature and rejects return to their earlier levels afterwards, the setting was the cause; if not, look again.

Motor Load, Cycle Time, Throughput and Blocking. When to consult: Elevated motor load, slower output, idle stations, queues, repeated blocked jobs or sudden stoppage. Possible causes: Normal job-to-job load variation, high cutting demand, speed selection, friction, tool wear, an upstream or downstream hold, or equipment breakdown. Recommended checks: Compare load during active work, not across long idle periods. Follow a specific job across station event records. Compare realized processing time with that station's usual cycle time, then identify whether completed work is waiting for the next station. Review running, idle and down states before blaming the machine with the visible queue. How to interpret: On this sequential line, a finished job can remain at one station until the next accepts it. A downstream bottleneck can create upstream delay without any upstream hardware fault. The second station has a relatively long nominal cycle and can be a normal bottleneck.

Material Batch Quality and Lot Traceability. When to consult: Inspection rejects cluster by batch or appear on jobs processed across several otherwise stable machines. Possible causes: Incoming stock variation, material hardness or contamination, a supplier or heat-treatment issue, cutting conditions, tooling, machine settings, or inspection randomness. Recommended checks: Group pass/fail results by batch ID; compare multiple jobs and adjacent batches. Trace representative rejected jobs through the line and check whether the same station or setting coincides with rejects. When possible, request material certificates, dimensional checks and receiving inspection rather than treating the lot number as an answer. How to interpret: Batch IDs connect material and finished jobs; a defect rate is statistical, so one failed inspection is weak evidence. A bad lot raises the share of rejects; it does not make every part fail, so jobs from that lot that pass inspection do not clear it, and an alternating or other pattern among a few jobs is usually chance. Judge a batch by its reject rate against other batches run through the same stations: a clearly higher rate in one batch points at the material even when some of its jobs pass. Material can be suspect even if equipment sensor trends remain normal, but also consider machine or inspection causes.

Tool Wear, Workholding and Cutting-Process Problems. When to consult: Declining surface finish, unstable cut, increased scrap, rising motor load or recurring vibration during particular jobs. Possible causes: Dull or damaged cutting tool, incorrect tool geometry, loose fixture, excessive feed, poor chip evacuation, material changes or spindle problems. Recommended checks: Compare results for different jobs, shifts and material batches; check operating speed, load and inspections. Request physical tool-edge, holder, fixture and chip-clearance inspections. Distinguish a cutting-only symptom from a mechanical problem that persists when the machine is not cutting. How to interpret: The available scalar sensors do not directly measure tool flank wear, cutting forces, surface roughness or fixture clamp force. Treat such diagnoses as possibilities until direct inspection or added instrumentation confirms them.

Sensor Drift, Dropout, Loose Probes and False Alarms. When to consult: Sudden single-sensor alarm, offset reading, gradually inconsistent sensor, intermittent missing samples, or a spike not shared by other measurements. Possible causes: Loose sensor mount, calibration drift, intermittent cable, communications loss, environmental interference, actual process upset or ordinary noise. Recommended checks: Count samples and inspect adjacent ticks: a missing point is not a zero reading. Compare the affected channel against its previous readings, parallel machine channels, factory air readings and event history. Ask whether independent measures (temperature, motor load, quality and status) corroborate the change. A technician may check sensor mounting, wiring and calibration. How to interpret: Do not equate an alarm with physical damage. A short disturbance that disappears and leaves other evidence stable may warrant observation rather than intervention. Repeated disagreement merits instrument investigation, not an automatic bearing replacement.

Ambient Air, Loading-Door and Shared Thermal Changes. When to consult: Several machines warm or cool together, or machine temperature changes around loading-door activity or daily operating periods. Possible causes: Factory air-temperature cycle, external weather or door exchange, ventilation changes, workload variation or independent machine faults. Recommended checks: Read the factory air thermometer and compare it with multiple machine temperatures in the same window. Check facility event records for door open and closed activity and compare machine status and load. Remember machine temperatures typically respond more slowly than surrounding air. How to interpret: A shared factory-level air change is a competing explanation for a machine temperature change. Do not diagnose a common bearing fault from several similar temperature changes without independent mechanical evidence.

Inspection Rejects, Maintenance Decisions and Verification. When to consult: Pass/fail outcomes worsen; alarms persist; a proposed fix is uncertain; a recent maintenance action appears not to help. Possible causes: Material or process changes, equipment wear, speed error, tool or fixture faults, inspection variation, or coincidental multiple causes. Recommended checks: Build a time-aligned record: affected machine and job IDs, batches, speeds, sensor trends, alarms, prior service and inspection results. State competing explanations and what evidence would separate them. Select an available action only when the expected improvement and potential downtime are justified; obtain human approval before execution. After maintenance, compare the same operating signals and inspection outcomes over a meaningful subsequent window. How to interpret: On this line, the only state-changing interventions are four approved repairs: a spindle-bearing replacement (§2.2), a speed-setting reset (§2.7), a feed-axis servo drive replacement (§2.14) and a hydraulic seal repair on a station fitted with hydraulics (§2.15). Each fixes one mechanism only; none repairs material, tooling or an instrument. Other physical checks may require a technician and are not available as actions. "Insufficient evidence" or "continue observing" are legitimate conclusions when the evidence does not separate the causes, but a fault that keeps worsening does not clear by being watched: wear and leaks progress until repaired. Completion of work is not proof the root cause was correct.

Feed-Axis Servo Drive: Following Error, Wear and Replacement. When to consult: A following-error alarm; following error rising over many readings on one station; parts from one station failing inspection for size while its vibration and temperature stay normal. Possible causes: A wearing feed-axis servo drive (amplifier, motor or its feedback), a heavy cut, a faster speed setting, a binding axis, or an instrument fault on the axis channel. Recommended checks: Following error is how far the feed axis lags behind the position the controller commands, measured by the servo controller itself on every move. A healthy drive keeps it small, a few micrometres at normal load; a heavier cut or a faster speed adds a little; while a station is idle or stopped the drive only holds the axis still and the lag falls to about one micrometre, so compare running periods only. The alarm fires above 20 µm. A wearing drive adds lag that grows slowly at first and then faster, and only while the station runs: a harder job wears it faster. Read the trend on the affected station over a long running window, and compare it with the same channel on other stations. Check power on the same station: a straining drive draws a little more. Check vibration, temperature and job times: a worn drive leaves them unchanged, while a worn spindle bearing raises vibration and heat and lengthens jobs (§2.2), and a wrong speed changes job times at one moment and then holds them steady (§2.7). Group inspection results by the station each failed job passed through: a drive fault follows the station across material batches, while a bad lot follows the batch across stations (§2.9). How to interpret: A lagging axis cuts parts off size, so more jobs from that station fail inspection, and the share grows as the drive wears; as with any defect rate, some of its jobs still pass (§2.9). A following error that keeps rising during production does not recover by itself and is not a transient: it keeps worsening until the drive is replaced, and an alarm that briefly clears is not evidence the drive is sound. The corrective action is an approved servo drive replacement, which takes the station out of service for about an hour; the maintenance record of the work states the condition of the drive removed, which is direct evidence of whether it was worn. Afterwards, following error during running work should return to a few micrometres and that station's rejects should fall back; if they do not, look again (an instrument, a binding axis or a second fault).

Hydraulic Clamping: Pressure Loss, Seal Leaks and Repair. When to consult: A low hydraulic-pressure alarm; hydraulic pressure falling over many readings on one station; workpieces shifting or parts failing inspection on a station fitted with hydraulics. Possible causes: Leaking hydraulic seals, a weakening pump, a sticking relief valve, an instrument fault on the pressure transducer, or normal draw during a heavy cut. Recommended checks: Only some stations have hydraulics; the machine list shows which. The pump holds a steady pressure whenever the station is powered, running or idle, and cutting draws only a few bar from it, so a sound system reads nearly flat. When a station is down, its hydraulic unit and transducer are switched off and send no readings: missing samples then are not a pressure loss. A seal leak lowers the pressure slowly at first and then faster, and unlike wear on the spindle or the feed axis it keeps growing while the station sits idle, because the pump keeps running. The low-pressure alarm fires when a reading falls below its setpoint, which the alarm event states. Read the pressure trend over a long window that includes idle periods, and compare idle readings with idle readings: a fall that persists while the station is not cutting is a leak, not a heavy cut. A pressure loss does not change vibration, temperature, following error or job times, which separates it from a bearing (§2.2), a drive (§2.14) or a speed setting (§2.7). Group inspection results by station and by batch as in §2.14. An erratic reading with gaps and no matching quality change points at the transducer instead (§2.11). How to interpret: Low clamping pressure lets the workpiece shift in the cut, so more jobs from that station fail inspection, and the share grows as the leak does; some of its jobs still pass (§2.9). A falling pressure does not recover by itself, and readings that briefly return above the setpoint during idle or light work do not clear it: the leak keeps growing until the seals are replaced. The corrective action is an approved hydraulic repair, possible only on a station fitted with hydraulics, which takes it out of service for about 40 ticks to replace the seals; the maintenance record of the work states the condition of the seals removed. Afterwards the pressure should return to its steady level and that station's rejects should fall back; if they do not, look again.
